title: Board-pattern readiness test — most-repeated question types
chapter: CBSE Class 10 Social Science (087) · Political Science: Democratic Politics II · Crash revision (2026-27)
tagline: Practice questions modelled on past CBSE papers; not predictions of this year's paper.
disclaimer: Original questions written from this video's script, its worksheet and the NCERT/CBSE material it cites, modelled on most-repeated / high-weightage question types in CBSE Sample Question Papers and past board papers. Practice for readiness only: not predictions of any exam and no promise of marks.
instructions: 39 questions. MCQ and assertion-reason: choose one option. Numeric: type a whole number.

S1.name: Power Sharing
S1.tip: Belgium (accommodation: equal ministers, state and community governments, Brussels) vs Sri Lanka (majoritarianism, 1956 Act). Prudential = less conflict; moral = spirit of democracy. Four forms: horizontal, vertical, social groups, parties and pressure groups.
S1.ncert: NCERT Democratic Politics II (Reprint 2026-27), Ch 1 Power Sharing

S2.name: Federalism
S2.tip: Three lists (Union, State, Concurrent) + residuary to the Union; clash on a Concurrent subject → Union law prevails. India is 'holding together'. 1992 amendment: regular elections, reservations, one-third seats for women, State Election Commission, shared powers and revenue.
S2.ncert: NCERT Democratic Politics II (Reprint 2026-27), Ch 2 Federalism

S3.name: Gender, Religion and Caste
S3.tip: Define patriarchy, sexual division of labour, communalism, secular state. Know women's representation facts (14.36% in 2019 Lok Sabha; 2023 Act: 33%). Three arguments why elections are not only about caste.
S3.ncert: NCERT Democratic Politics II (Reprint 2026-27), Ch 3 Gender, Religion and Caste

S4.name: Political Parties
S4.tip: Seven functions in order, three components, party systems with examples, four challenges and the reforms already made vs suggested. 5-markers: 5 points, one line each, ≤ 120 words.
S4.ncert: NCERT Democratic Politics II (Reprint 2026-27), Ch 4 Political Parties

S5.name: Outcomes of Democracy
S5.tip: Democracy creates conditions; citizens use them. Judge it as accountable, responsive and legitimate. Growth: dictatorships slightly ahead (4.42% vs 3.95%), negligible among poor countries. Weak on inequality; strong on dignity and freedom.
S5.ncert: NCERT Democratic Politics II (Reprint 2026-27), Ch 5 Outcomes of Democracy

questions.question: What percentage of Belgium's people live in the Flemish region and speak Dutch?
questions.explanation: Belgium: 59% Dutch-speaking (Flemish region), 40% French-speaking (Wallonia), 1% German-speaking.
questions.remediation: Video part 1: Power Sharing; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: In Brussels, the capital of Belgium, the situation is different from the country as a whole because:
questions.explanation: Dutch speakers are the national majority, but French speakers are 80% in Brussels.
questions.remediation: Video part 1: Power Sharing; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: About 80% speak French and 20% speak Dutch

questions.question: What did the 1956 Act in Sri Lanka do?
questions.explanation: The Act was a majoritarian measure that alienated Sri Lankan Tamils.
questions.remediation: Video part 1: Power Sharing; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: It made Tamil the only official language
It divided power between the centre and the provinces
It created a community government for Tamils
It recognised Sinhala as the only official language

questions.question: Majoritarianism means:
questions.explanation: Sri Lanka's post-1948 governments followed majoritarian measures.
questions.remediation: Video part 1: Power Sharing; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: Power is shared equally among all communities
The minority community governs the majority
The majority community rules the country in whatever way it wants, ignoring the wishes and needs of the minority
Every decision needs a two-thirds majority

questions.question: Choose the correct option.
questions.explanation: Both true, but R is the moral reason, while A states the prudential reason; R does not explain A.
questions.remediation: Video part 1: Power Sharing; then the worksheet practice for this part.
questions.assertion: Power sharing reduces the possibility of conflict between social groups.
questions.reason: Power sharing is the very spirit of democracy.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.question: Power shared among the legislature, executive and judiciary, with checks and balances, is called:
questions.explanation: Horizontal: organs at the same level; vertical: levels of government (centre, state, local).
questions.remediation: Video part 1: Power Sharing; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: Which is an example of VERTICAL division of power?
questions.explanation: Vertical = between higher and lower levels of government.
questions.remediation: Video part 1: Power Sharing; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: Power shared among the central, state and local governments
Power shared among legislature, executive and judiciary

questions.question: In Belgium, a question about the language of instruction in Dutch-speaking schools would be decided mainly by:
questions.explanation: The community government, elected by each language group, handles cultural, educational and language issues.
questions.remediation: Video part 1: Power Sharing; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: The community government elected by the Dutch-speaking people

questions.question: Which subject is in the Union List?
questions.explanation: Union: defence, foreign affairs, banking, communications, currency. Police, agriculture and irrigation are State subjects.
questions.remediation: Video part 2: Federalism; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: Which subject is in the Concurrent List?
questions.explanation: Concurrent: education, forest, trade unions, marriage, adoption, succession.
questions.remediation: Video part 2: Federalism; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: Who can make laws on 'residuary' subjects like computer software?
questions.explanation: Residuary subjects, not in any list, go to the Union.
questions.remediation: Video part 2: Federalism; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: Choose the correct option.
questions.explanation: Both true, but R only lists Concurrent subjects; it does not explain why the Union law prevails.
questions.remediation: Video part 2: Federalism; then the worksheet practice for this part.
questions.assertion: If Union and State laws on a Concurrent List subject conflict, the Union law prevails.
questions.reason: The Concurrent List includes subjects like education, forest and marriage.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.question: India, Spain and Belgium are examples of which kind of federation?
questions.explanation: Holding together: a large country divides power, and the centre tends to be stronger. Coming together: USA, Switzerland, Australia.
questions.remediation: Video part 2: Federalism; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: What is needed to change the basic division of powers between the Union and the States?
questions.explanation: Fundamental provisions cannot be changed by one level alone; courts act as umpire in disputes.
questions.remediation: Video part 2: Federalism; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: A decision of the Prime Minister alone
A simple majority in one House
An order of the State Election Commission
A two-thirds majority in both Houses of Parliament and ratification by at least half of the states

questions.question: Which of these was NOT a provision of the 1992 amendment on local government?
questions.explanation: Regular elections became constitutionally mandatory, so indefinite postponement is the opposite of the amendment.
questions.remediation: Video part 2: Federalism; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: State governments may postpone local body elections indefinitely
At least one-third of positions are reserved for women
Regular elections to local bodies are mandatory
A State Election Commission conducts local elections

questions.question: Who heads a municipal corporation?
questions.explanation: Municipal corporations (big cities) are headed by a mayor; the gram panchayat by a sarpanch.
questions.remediation: Video part 2: Federalism; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: Patriarchy is:
questions.explanation: Literally 'rule by father'; a feminist believes in equal rights and opportunities for women and men.
questions.remediation: Video part 3: Gender, Religion and Caste; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: A system of equal rights for all
A system that values men more and gives them power over women

questions.question: The 'sexual division of labour' refers to:
questions.explanation: Housework is left to women, and that work stays unpaid and invisible.
questions.remediation: Video part 3: Gender, Religion and Caste; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: A system in which all work inside the home is done, or organised, by women
Separate schools for boys and girls
Men doing all paid and unpaid work

questions.question: In 2019, women's share in the Lok Sabha touched for the first time:
questions.explanation: 14.36% in 2019; the Women's Reservation Act 2023 provides 33% in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies.
questions.remediation: Video part 3: Gender, Religion and Caste; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: What percentage of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies does the Women's Reservation Act of 2023 (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) provide for women?
questions.explanation: 33% (one-third) of seats.
questions.remediation: Video part 3: Gender, Religion and Caste; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: Which group of countries has a high level of women's participation in public life?
questions.explanation: The Nordic countries lead in women's participation.
questions.remediation: Video part 3: Gender, Religion and Caste; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: Which is a feature of India as a secular state?
questions.explanation: No official religion; freedom to profess, practise and propagate; no discrimination; intervention for equality (e.g. banning untouchability).
questions.remediation: Video part 3: Gender, Religion and Caste; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: Only one religion may be propagated
The state can never intervene in religious matters
There is no official religion, and the state may intervene in religion to ensure equality

questions.question: Communalism means:
questions.explanation: It shows up as everyday prejudice, quest for dominance, religious mobilisation and violence.
questions.remediation: Video part 3: Gender, Religion and Caste; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: Using religion in politics in exclusive and partisan terms

questions.question: Which argument best shows that elections in India are NOT only about caste?
questions.explanation: Parties and candidates must win the trust of more than one caste, and voters also weigh other issues.
questions.remediation: Video part 3: Gender, Religion and Caste; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: No parliamentary constituency has a clear majority of one single caste
Every party gets all the votes of one caste

questions.question: The three components of a political party are:
questions.explanation: Leaders, active members and followers.
questions.remediation: Video part 4: Political Parties; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a function of political parties?
questions.explanation: Seven functions: contest elections, put forward policies, make laws, form governments, act as opposition, shape opinion, give access to welfare schemes.
questions.remediation: Video part 4: Political Parties; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: Appointing judges of the Supreme Court

questions.question: Which country is an example of a two-party system?
questions.explanation: One-party: China; two-party: USA, UK; multiparty: India.
questions.remediation: Video part 4: Political Parties; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: As per the Election Commission's 2023 notification mentioned in the video, how many recognised national parties are there?
questions.explanation: Six recognised national parties, recognised on their share of votes and seats.
questions.remediation: Video part 4: Political Parties; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: Why has India evolved a multiparty system?
questions.explanation: Diversity explains the multiparty system.
questions.remediation: Video part 4: Political Parties; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: Its social and geographical diversity cannot easily be absorbed by two or three parties
Only one party is allowed to rule
Every state has its own Constitution

questions.question: Choose the correct option.
questions.explanation: Both true, and R explains A.
questions.remediation: Video part 4: Political Parties; then the worksheet practice for this part.
questions.assertion: Political parties are necessary in a representative democracy.
questions.reason: Without parties, every candidate would be independent and nobody would be responsible for how the country is run.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.question: Which challenge to political parties does 'dynastic succession' describe?
questions.explanation: Four challenges: lack of internal democracy, dynastic succession, money and muscle power, lack of meaningful choice.
questions.remediation: Video part 4: Political Parties; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: Top positions are passed on to members of one family

questions.question: Which of these steps to reform parties has ALREADY been taken, rather than only suggested?
questions.explanation: Made: anti-defection law, affidavits ordered by the Supreme Court, EC order on organisational elections and tax returns. The others are suggestions.
questions.remediation: Video part 4: Political Parties; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: Reserving one-third of party tickets for women
A law to regulate parties' internal affairs

questions.question: Democracy is expected to produce a government that is:
questions.explanation: Outcome one: an accountable, responsive and legitimate government.
questions.remediation: Video part 5: Outcomes of Democracy; then the worksheet practice for this part.

questions.question: According to data for 1950–2000, which statement about economic growth is correct?
questions.explanation: 4.42% vs 3.95%; among poor countries the gap is negligible (4.34% vs 4.28%).
questions.remediation: Video part 5: Outcomes of Democracy; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: Democracies grew much faster than dictatorships
Dictatorships grew slightly faster (4.42%) than democracies (3.95%)
Dictatorships did not grow at all

questions.question: Choose the correct option.
questions.explanation: Both true, and R explains A: growth depends on other factors too.
questions.remediation: Video part 5: Outcomes of Democracy; then the worksheet practice for this part.
questions.assertion: Economic growth alone cannot be the reason to prefer dictatorship over democracy.
questions.reason: Among poor countries, the difference in growth rates between dictatorships and democracies is negligible.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.question: In countries like South Africa and Brazil, the top 20% of people take more than 60% of the national income. This shows that democracies:
questions.explanation: Outcome three: on inequality and poverty, democracies have not done well.
questions.remediation: Video part 5: Outcomes of Democracy; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: Have not done well in reducing economic inequality
Do not allow anyone to be rich

questions.question: For democracy to accommodate social diversity, which condition is necessary?
questions.explanation: Both conditions from the chapter.
questions.remediation: Video part 5: Outcomes of Democracy; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: The majority must work with the minority, and rule by majority must not become rule by one religious, racial or language community
The largest community must always rule
All languages except one must be banned

questions.question: Which feature makes decisions in a democracy transparent?
questions.explanation: Decisions follow norms and procedures, and citizens can find out how they were made.
questions.remediation: Video part 5: Outcomes of Democracy; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: Secret decisions by a few leaders
Citizens' right to information about how decisions are taken

questions.question: People in democracies often complain about their governments. What does this show?
questions.explanation: Democracy's examination never gets over; complaints show citizens have become aware and critical.
questions.remediation: Video part 5: Outcomes of Democracy; then the worksheet practice for this part.
options: Citizens have become aware and expect more, which itself is a sign of democracy's success
Complaints are not allowed in a democracy
